title: What Makes Learning Stick
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Based on a conversation with Pete Mattock on the Leading With podcast, this article identifies key principles for making learning stick: prioritizing depth over breadth in the curriculum, establishing the architectural big ideas before filling in content, and harnessing the power of narrative and being read aloud as pedagogical tools. The central problem is that schools try to cover too much content, producing a curriculum that is a mile wide and an inch thick—preventing students from exploring bigger concepts or developing deep meaning. Leaders must identify purpose statements in each subject before the programmes of study, since these reveal the big ideas that make new knowledge memorable and meaningful. Evidence from the University of Sussex's Faster Read study is cited: 12 weeks of teachers reading aloud while pupils follow along increased reading ages by 8.5 months on average, and 16 months for lower-attaining readers. The essay also addresses the KS2-KS3 transition as a systemic failure point where secondary schools routinely ignore primary learning, sometimes reteaching Year 4 content in Year 7 as though it were new.
points: Schools that misstep on curriculum typically try to do too much, producing a curriculum a mile wide and an inch thick—preventing depth of meaning and the exploration of big ideas that make knowledge memorable.

The architectural sequence matters: leaders should identify purpose statements and big ideas in each subject before the programmes of study, because once big ideas are established, new knowledge becomes stickier and more meaningfully organized.

The University of Sussex's Faster Read study found that 12 weeks of teachers reading aloud while pupils followed along increased reading ages by 8.5 months on average, and nearly 16 months for lower-attaining readers.

The KS2-KS3 transition is a systemic failure: secondary year-7 curriculum often ignores what children learned in primary school, with some schools reteaching Year 4 content in Year 7 as though it were new—insulting to primary colleagues and demoralizing for students.
High-quality curriculum texts should provoke curiosity, treat children as intelligent human beings, and contain rich vocabulary that does the heavy lifting of learning.
quotes: A curriculum that’s a mile wide and an inch thick, as Dylan Wiliam would say.
Children don’t get the chance to explore bigger concepts because we’re ploughing through to cover everything. We need to think less about coverage and more about depth of meaning.
What we should be doing first is looking at the purpose statements — those beautifully framed intentions about the difference a subject makes to young people’s lives.

Schools tapping into research on narrative are seeing remarkable results. The University of Sussex's Faster Read study found that over 12 weeks of teachers reading aloud while pupils followed along, reading ages increased by 8.5 months. For lower-attaining readers, it was nearly double: 16 months.
When asked why they'd done so well, pupils said: 'We don't normally get the chance to do this interesting work.'
What goes wrong at key stage three is that senior leaders and subject leaders aren’t asking: what have children learned up until this point?
We wonder why children switch off. But it’s also insulting to primary colleagues, because it is dismissing rather than honouring their work.
